title: One question, a useful plan
summary: A good first answer gives you something to work with. A good follow-up changes what happens next.
description: How a small editorial question becomes a practical repair plan through discovery, computation and a follow-up.
body:
An editor asks which articles need attention. The first useful answer is a short list of gaps: a missing description here, an image without alternative text there. It gives the team a place to begin.

Then the question changes. Which fixes would help the most readers? Now the work involves finding shared assets and grouping the affected articles. The underlying content is the same, but the calculation is different.

That is the interesting part of working with an agent: the conversation can reshape the computation. Keep the tools small, make their permissions explicit, and let the next question determine how they are combined.

title: The quiet work of a good API
summary: Predictable inputs, bounded results and clear failures give a small API room to grow.
description: A few habits that make application tools easier to compose and safer to call.
body:
The best part of a useful API is often what you stop thinking about. You know which arguments it accepts, what the result means and how much data a call can return.

We start with typed inputs and a deliberately small response. A content read returns the fields the caller needs. Pagination has a limit. Missing records and denied access have a defined outcome.

Those details matter when software calls the API automatically. A tool that behaves predictably becomes a building block for several workflows, without needing a different endpoint for every new question.

title: A week of small improvements
summary: The improvements that made our sample journal easier to use were mostly small and specific.
body:
This week's editorial exercise began with the ordinary things: clearer titles, shorter introductions and a few links that needed another look. Each change was easy to explain on its own.

Together they made the journal easier to scan. Readers could choose an article from its summary, and editors could see which pages still needed attention.

We kept a list of what changed and why. It became a useful starting point for the next review, especially when a small fix applied to several pages. The lesson was simple: make the work visible enough that someone else can continue it.

title: Shared images need shared ownership
summary: A shared asset can connect several articles. Its repair deserves the same wider view.
description: Why an editorial repair plan should consider how shared media is used across a site.
body:
An image can appear on an event page, a news story and a guide. That reuse is convenient until nobody knows who owns the description or which pages depend on it.

An editorial review should follow those references. Before suggesting a change, check whether the alternative text is shared on the media item or stored separately at each use. The answer changes the repair plan.

Counting references can help prioritize the work, but it is only part of the decision. Context still matters: an image may serve a different purpose on each page. A good report makes those relationships visible for an editor to review.

title: Tell readers what comes next
summary: A description is a small promise about the page someone is about to open.
body:
A title names the subject. A useful description gives the reader a reason to continue. It can explain who the article is for, the question it answers or the practical detail it contains.

Writing that sentence is harder when the article tries to do too much. We often discover a better introduction while trying to summarize the page.

For an automated review, finding an empty description is a clear starting point. Deciding whether a filled description is useful needs more context. Keep those two findings separate so an editor can distinguish missing data from a judgment that deserves discussion.

title: Make the busy days boring
summary: Background work becomes easier to operate when its limits and failure states are visible.
description: Notes on keeping background processing understandable, bounded and recoverable.
body:
Some work can finish after the page response: a report, an import or a notification. Moving it into a worker gives the application a different place to manage time and resource limits.

That worker still needs a clear contract. We want to know what started, what completed and whether retrying could repeat an effect. A timeout tells us that waiting stopped; it does not tell us that nothing happened.

For a read-only audit, this is a manageable starting point. Record the calls, keep the workload bounded and return a report that explains any incomplete work.

title: Accessibility starts before the template
summary: Content decisions shape how a page works long before someone chooses its layout.
body:
A readable page begins with content choices: a descriptive heading, a clear link label and an explanation for an image that carries information. A theme can support those choices, but it cannot make them for the editor.

Our sample review looks for concrete omissions first. An empty alternative-text field is something to investigate, not an automatic instruction to invent a description. Some images are decorative; others need their surrounding context.

The useful output is a review queue with enough information to make a decision. Editors should be able to see the affected pages and understand why each item was included.

title: Leave an experiment someone can repeat
summary: A result becomes more useful when another person can reproduce the conditions behind it.
description: What to keep with a technical demonstration so another developer can verify its result.
body:
An impressive number is a starting point for questions. What was counted? Which input was used? Did both approaches do the same work?

We keep those details alongside the experiment: the submitted program, the tool calls, the returned data and the limits applied to the run. A result without those details is difficult to compare later.

Repeatability also means respecting the person's time. A small fixture and a clear command are more useful than a long setup story. When a dependency or runtime is missing, the command should say so and stop before producing a misleading result.

title: A useful failure leaves evidence
summary: A refused request and an unavailable service can look similar until you inspect what happened.
description: Why a security demonstration should connect the execution trace to the application's own access decision.
body:
A request returned no content. That is useful to know, but it is not yet proof that access control worked. The service might have been unavailable, or the request might have contained an invalid argument.

To understand the outcome, follow the evidence across the boundary. Did the tool receive the request? Which account did the application evaluate? Was the read actually denied?

A small, deliberate negative case can answer those questions. Keep the record safe: log the decision and the identifiers needed to correlate it, while leaving restricted content out of both the response and the log.

title: When a summary is enough
summary: Sometimes the result needs to cross the boundary, while the intermediate data can stay where it was processed.
body:
Suppose a question asks for the number of articles missing a description. Reading the metadata is necessary; returning every article body is not.

A program can inspect the records, count the gaps and return a compact result. A follow-up might need a different shape: perhaps IDs and titles, or groups ordered by impact.

Measure the difference carefully. Smaller serialized results do not by themselves establish lower model cost or faster overall execution. Record what actually crossed the tool boundary and keep that measurement separate from provider usage and elapsed time.

title: Make the next change easier
summary: A useful abstraction earns its place when the next integration needs less special treatment.
description: Keeping execution, authorization and application-specific tools separate as a project grows.
body:
The first integration teaches us what the application needs. The second shows which assumptions were accidental.

We try to keep the reusable parts clear: the execution boundary, the tool contract and the record of what happened. An application's content model and permission rules belong close to that application.

This makes the next change easier to evaluate. Adding a content source should not require teaching the sandbox how that CMS stores nodes or media. It should require a small set of approved tools with explicit inputs, outputs and access checks.

title: Before you press publish
summary: A short final review can catch the omissions that are easiest to miss while writing.
description: A practical editorial review of titles, descriptions, links and image context before publication.
body:
Read the title and introduction together. Do they describe the same article? Check the description next: does it help someone decide whether the page is relevant?

Follow the links that carry the argument. Look at images with their surrounding text and consider whether their alternative text serves that context. If an asset is shared, identify the other pages that a change could affect.

Automation can collect the candidates and organize the work. Publication remains an editorial decision. A good checklist makes that decision easier without pretending that every judgment is a missing-field check.

title: Autumn editorial plan — draft
summary: An unpublished planning note reserved for the editorial team.
body:
This synthetic draft belongs to the editorial team. It sketches a future series about maintaining a small technical journal.

The read-only demo account must not receive its title or body through the article tool. Publishing it requires a separate editorial action.

title: Release retrospective — draft
body:
This synthetic draft collects questions for a release retrospective: what surprised the team, which checks helped and where documentation was missing.

It is intentionally unpublished so the demo has realistic restricted content beyond the original security fixture.

title: Agent workshop outline — draft
summary: An unpublished workshop outline for a later session.
body:
This synthetic workshop outline explores a short conversation: inspect a dataset, ask a follow-up and verify the resulting computation.

The outline remains a draft. An agent using the read-only content account must respect that state even when it knows the node ID.
